en: The Sutra on the Causes and Conditions of King Aśoka’s Son Losing His Eyes, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Dharmanandi of the Fu Qin Dynasty.
People have been entangled in birth and death for a long time; their habitual transgressions and consciousness are deep-rooted.
From the arising of affliction and turmoil, lust becomes a disease;
it inevitably results in turbulent surges like a river in flood, causing injury and ruin.
The wise person holds fast to their mind with clear discernment, maintaining a state of detachment and self-restraint, thereby governing the sources of all evils.
The twenty-one fetters defile the human mind; all should be abandoned, lest one fall back into heedless conduct.
Let us all with one mind listen to what I say regarding King Aśoka’s tranquility—the source of his impaired vision, whose fame reaches the eight quarters.
Pervading the boundaries of the kingdom, the multitudes were in a state of great agitation; none failed to be struck with wonder.
The Holy King Aśoka governed and transformed them from within, leading all the realms of Jambudvīpa so that none did not obey his commands.
The king further begot a son, whose countenance was upright and handsome.
Born with marks of nobility, he was destined to succeed to the royal throne.
His eyes were clear and bright like those of a celestial lord. When the king beheld this transformation, he was immeasurably delighted;
he immediately summoned his ministers, śramaṇas, and practitioners of the Way, personally embracing the child to show him to them.
He had them examine his features and further commanded his ministers:
"Bestow upon him another name so that it may be celebrated throughout the world and its fame heard in all directions.
The ministers bowed their heads in obeisance and received the command, saying: "The King has fathered a noble son, a rarity in this world."
"By means of the True Dharma, this divine being has descended from heaven. We shall now establish his name as Dharmavardhana.
The reason for this is that because the royal law is orderly, he shall instruct the people through the Dharma;
he never departs from principle, and we are truly his [disciples]."
A true son of the Dharma, he is thus called a noble son; his name is Dharmavardhana, and his eyes are like lotus flowers.
All who see him rejoice; when he looks upon others, his eyes blink like those of King Indradyumna.
His speech is delivered with careful deliberation, neither too slow nor too hurried.
By nature gentle and mild, he did not act with sudden violence.
His fame and virtue were such that they could not be fully recorded; now they shall be recounted once more:
he was known as Candana, and King Aśoka held him in the highest esteem and affection, providing for his care and sustenance at all times.
Lest there be any misfortune, the King constantly dispatched scouts;
having investigated and ascertained through secret informants that his son was auspicious, he would then partake of food.
He would personally embrace Dharmika, delighting in playing with him all day long; moved by affection and pity, he never grew weary of him whether awake or asleep.
The Dharma-benefactor spoke these words: "What merit have you cultivated that you now possess eyes like the *utpala* flower?

Whether you are in a garden or traveling through the borders of the kingdom, I shall always provide you with protection so that you do not suffer grief, along with all the men and women who accompany you."
Seeing the celestial maidens arrive, they all gave rise to perverse thoughts and conceived lustful desires.
The King was by nature particularly attached to female beauty;
the attendants of the inner palace were like celestial nymphs, and all the women therein harbored seductive charms in their hearts.
Elegant and lovely, there was none she had not mastered through her training.
The King’s concubine was named Jingrong; day and night she waited and watched, wishing to have illicit relations with me.
On what day shall my wish finally be fulfilled, that I may obtain the Heavenly Eye?
Wandering together in leisure and tranquility, their minds were immediately satisfied;
they did not envy the celestial palaces, for even as their bodies were thus perishing, they harbored no resentment toward the world.
At that time, the King’s Crown Prince rose early in the morning and went to the Lady’s quarters, where he knelt, prostrated, and inquired after her well-being.
Your rising and resting are light and easy; your walking is tireless.
Furthermore, you present these sweet and auspicious fruits. When the lady saw him approaching, her desire blazed up, and she said:
"Come before me; let us enjoy ourselves together, so that my wish may be fulfilled."
Furthermore, when kinship ends and both self and other share in mutual joy, is that not indeed a source of delight?
When the Deva with the Celestial Eye heard this, he covered his ears with his hands and reflected within himself:
"How cruel are these words! What a most grievous calamity; how piercing is the pain through my heart!"
"The kindness of his upbringing is so profound; how could I allow this dharma to cause him to gradually retreat and return the way he came?
He has returned to his own place, practicing in silent seclusion.
Seeing that his wishes have been thwarted, he has severed all hope and sighs with grief, beating his breast."
Conceiving a malicious intent, with disheveled hair and matted locks, he sits upon the ground;
bound by rage like a rākṣasa demon, how could that man take me and humiliate me?
I must certainly employ skillful means to gouge out both his eyes.
He caused it so that within these borders there were none who could see or hear him, let alone men or women beholding his physical form.
At that time, there was a minister named Yaśas, whom the father-king relied upon;
he subdued the myriad people with his majesty at the beginning of the spring festival.
They have come to offer congratulations; they pay their respects with the ritual bows and courtesies of former times.
When the Prince saw them approaching, he struck his head with his hand, saying:
"An omen of ill fortune stands before me! Return quickly to your original place; do not remain here any longer."
"I wish to enter the court to offer congratulations to Your Majesty.
Your servant shall seek and grasp Your Hand, feigning profound reverence; I pray that the Prince may enjoy infinite longevity.
Having used Your Majesty’s hand to strike my head, [I feel] this body of mine is soft and supple.
Without causing him any harm, he spoke slowly with a smile;
yet inwardly, his mind was filled with resentment and anger, like a serpent harboring venom.
He thought to himself in secret that he must avenge this grudge, and until that right hand fell, he would never again walk in this world.
Having knelt, Yaśas withdrew to his place and reported these original facts to the Queen Mother.
The Lady then replied: "Listen to my words; there are indeed stains [upon you], and out of shame I cannot speak of them—the insults and humiliations he has inflicted."
What place could contain it? It divides itself to receive the severing of its form; it never ceases to abandon [its nature], just like Yaśas.
Fire produced within water burns and consumes mountains, wilds, cities, and towns.
When people see this, there are none who are not struck with wonder and alarm.
The ministers faced one another and discussed together:
"How could it be that fire has arisen within the water today? Water is able to extinguish fire, yet now fire is produced from within it.
This royal lineage is likewise like this metaphor; having encountered this Prince..."

Like fire arising from water, it burns my heart. Though the merits I have cultivated were originally free from fear, I now experience dread. Throughout the long night, I have constantly harbored this thought:
"My years are advanced in age; I must surely obtain the strength of a son."
On the contrary, he further humiliated me, treating me like a plaything for a harlot. This matter remains concealed;

to whom else should I appeal? Yaśas spoke: "Your transgression deserves punishment, and you have brought disgrace upon your majesty and insulted your servant. You must act now; devise a clever stratagem."
Seeking the appropriate means, he did not gouge out both eyes; thus it was not the time for requiting an enmity.
At that time there was an Arhat named Shan-nian (Good Thought), whose divine eye was honored by the teachers and the people.
When the True Man entered meditative concentration, he observed with the power of the Way.
The Prince shall later inevitably encounter the conditions and consequences [of his past deeds].
Repeatedly instructing him with subtle teachings of the Way, he causes him to understand the shifting of circumstances.
He explains to the Prince that all things return to emptiness, and that even form does not exist; neither existence nor non-existence exists.
Non-existence is also non-existent; sound responds from without. By means of the internal faculty of the ear, fragrance wafts forth on its own;
the nose-consciousness receives it. Various flavors pass through the mouth, further increasing the activity of the tongue-root.
The body craves smoothness and softness; the mind and its objects never reach satiety.
If phenomena exist, they also exist; if phenomena do not exist, they also do not exist.
When there is neither existence nor non-existence, even non-non-existence does not exist. They are like a mass of foam, destined to perish;
the eye has no permanent master and cannot be preserved for long, being like a bubble upon the water.
All things ultimately return to decay; one should contemplate and reflect upon this.
The transformations of impermanence cause the eyes to shift and change; rise and fall do not cease.
One should exert oneself and strive for the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); for that divine eye cannot be destroyed or ruined.

Gradually you shall arrive at that place free from sorrow; frequently relinquishing worldly affairs, go to listen to the words of the Dharma, associate with virtuous friends, and engage in fellowship with them.
Upon hearing the Dharma, your mind will awaken, and your eyes will attain purity through the influence of these excellent spiritual friends.
Upon attaining arhatship, one focuses the mind on the Buddha,
contemplates the Dharma-treasure, and reverently serves the Sangha, as well as teachers and elders. With an unshakable mind,
one encounters the Greatly Attained, dwells in the Immovable Ground, and becomes a true son of the Buddha.
Upon hearing this, Fayi was moved by a mixture of sorrow and joy, thinking: "There must be a cause for this;
it shall not be in vain. How is it that the human body—and even the eye—is impermanent?
My teacher now issues this admonition with such profound earnestness; I ought to guard myself accordingly."
If one practices severe teachings, how could one dare to be negligent or disrespectful?

One would be violating my Holy Teacher. At that time, within Jambudvīpa, at the place where the Bodhisattva practiced the act of casting himself down, there was a stone chamber named Śilāgṛha, where a king constantly ruled.

When they encountered the destruction of the kingdom and the death of their sovereign, the ministers and commoners of the realm, both great and small, all went together to the place where King Aśoka was;
prostrating themselves before him with reverence, they joined their palms and said: "May the Holy King prolong his life!"
To promote prosperity and ensure robust health; The King of the Stone Chamber disperses his rule.
Relinquishing the throne to transfer his spirit, he prays for a proper succession To lead the remaining people of the wilderness. The King then looked back and addressed Yaśas, saying:
"Quickly issue orders for the dispatch of officials; Who should be appointed to preside over them?"
"The people there are fierce and stubborn; one must be capable to govern them.
Do not allow an ordinary man to take charge of that land. Yaśas thought to himself, "Now is the very time to send Prince Dharmavardhana to take charge. He immediately knelt down before [the King].
He then addressed the King, saying: "I pray that you will grant me your permission.
What Your humble servant reports is that the kingdom of Gandhāra is as delightful as a celestial palace.
I pray that you dispatch the Prince to govern the remaining wild inhabitants; thus shall he bring about a profound transformation in that land."
"Furthermore, let the imperial majesty cause its far-reaching resonance to reach beyond all boundaries.
Upon hearing this, the Father King immediately became enraged and said: "Alas, what you have proposed is foolish! How could it be fit to report to the Emperor?
You are neither the sovereign of the state nor a leader of the people; by what power do you act thus?"
"Let my breath depart! What is the use of your tongue? It would be better for it to fall off piece by piece than for you to seek to send me away—me, the child still within the womb.
Now, I grant you again the pardon for your crime of killing; mend your ways and reform yourself, lest you perish at my hand."
From now until the end, I reprimand and charge you once more: guard your clans with care so that you may attain the Mandate of Heaven.
Should anyone dare to utter my name or title, I shall personally take up the sword and strike off your heads. If there should be yet others...
Those who address me by name shall have their tongues plucked out at birth,
and I shall take them as food. Even if they were my sons, or those with whom you had enmity in the past—
due to the roots of causes and conditions created in the past, as well as in the present through the actions of body, speech, and mind.
Now, may you grant full pardon and not record my former offenses. At that time, the minister harbored resentment and disregarded his own life;
he again knelt before [the king] and earnestly declared the truth: "Excellent, Great King!
I pray that you will exercise your sovereign majesty and deign to reflect upon this with care."
To ensure that the state remains undisturbed: the people of the West are by nature volatile and constantly prone to strife and litigation;

they raise armies for offensive warfare. It is fitting that you employ virtuous transformation to pacify and win over their hearts, so that the ministers may be harmonious and concordant—is this not indeed a most auspicious occasion?
In the kingdom of Gandhāra, there abound rare treasures and many jewels;
its inhabitants are of lofty talent and vast learning, skilled in all matters.
Furthermore, in the city of Śaila-guhā, where King Puṣpamālya once ruled, his fame remains undecaying; there, in the royal park, lies a pond.
Born from golden lotuses with silver leaves and jeweled stalks, its value exceeds that of Jambudvīpa.
This city possesses majesty and immeasurable divine virtue; it is not a place where ordinary persons may venture.
Though the kingdom lies at the western frontier, its affairs are increasingly abundant and vast.
I pray that Your Majesty will examine this well and not neglect these humble words.
It is because the affairs of state are so weighty that I have repeatedly petitioned you; how could I dare to act solely on my own initiative?
May Your Majesty cause the Crown Prince to develop his sharp faculties and wisdom, so that he may fully understand all phenomena as well as the arts of warfare and combat.
Fully prepared and thoroughly practiced, should he encounter the prince in that land, he will not employ the sword or staff;
he will naturally subdue him. His speech is gentle and free from coarseness;
his nature is broad and benevolent, and he possesses no heart of greed or stinginess.
Do not let wine pass your lips; exercise self-restraint regarding sensual desires; extend kindness through universal love and govern without partiality.
If you do not possess these virtues, how could I, as a subject, presume to announce them?
Therefore, I have troubled Your Majesty’s hearing with this; I pray that you will grant me leave at once, so that Your Majesty may focus your mind exclusively [upon this].

What need is there for these two worries? If you contemplate the breath of the Honored One, consider that if you do not plan for the present state of that kingdom, there will surely be calamity later.
When affairs are not foreseen, ruin occurs in an instant. Upon hearing these words, the King was as if choking on his food.
Having neither entered his belly nor being able to vomit it out, he was so deluded by the great minister that no one realized what had happened;
he was like a moth leaping into a flame, heedless of its future consequences.
At that time, King Aśoka shed tears and commanded that Dharmavivardhana be sent as a messenger.
He governed that land with tens of thousands of close ministers who naturally responded to his auspicious treasures;
these soon gathered at the celestial court. King Aśoka personally took up the royal crown in his own hands, placed it upon the head of Dharmarakṣita, and addressed him, saying:
Excellent, O new king! May there be auspiciousness and nothing but benefit.

May you always cause my lineage to ascend to this honorable position. Let bells be struck and drums beaten, and let hundreds and thousands of kinds of performances and music be performed, with hanging silk banners and canopies, throughout that land.
There was nowhere it did not pervade within eight *yojanas*, filled with people,
armored elephants, and horses— each numbering eighty-four thousand. Adorned with interlacing gold and silver beyond measure,
there were eighty-four thousand chariots made of precious gems and feathers.
The host of infantry numbered eighty-four thousand;
like the Lord of Devas departing for the rear garden with a retinue of jade maidens, what music could surpass such as this?
Thus the prince, having reached that region, entered the city of Śilāgṛha.
With a countless retinue, the King arrived at the borders of his kingdom;
the myriad people raised cries of celebration, their hearts filled with joy as they amused themselves as if in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Within the city, along the streets and alleys, silk banners and canopies were suspended, and fragrant liquid was sprinkled upon the ground, pervading every place without exception.
At that time, King Dharmavardhana addressed the people, saying:
"O you who honor me with sincerity, for seven days do not engage in any work;
I shall bestow upon you treasures and wealth such as those found within my own palace."
Delighting in the five pleasures, indulging in play at will, day and night without weariness—I now bestow upon you treasures to be used as you please.
Even if you should incur debts, these goods shall serve as repayment; should you fall into misfortune, you need not become a slave to others.
Bestow wealth and silk upon them, and exempt them from labor service.
Command all men and women, great and small within the city, to universally practice virtue; let there be no resentment.
Furthermore, issue my edict to the regions beyond, that for six years henceforth, [they shall likewise observe this].
Do not let them lose their wealth and property; should there be those who are orphaned, destitute, or utterly impoverished, I shall also bestow goods upon them so that they lack for nothing.
Those who are able to cultivate themselves and harbor no intent to kill or steal, I shall honor and receive them as if they were no different from myself.
At that time, King Fayi proclaimed again, saying: "The three fast days of each half-month are difficult to encounter.
Men and women, exhort one another not to give rise to indolence, but to uphold the Eight Precepts.
This is the fasting dharma of the Tathāgata; the Buddha has taught that such is the human body."
Only after billions of kalpas may one obtain [this opportunity], avoiding the eight states of no leisure.
Like a plank floating on the ocean meeting a blind turtle’s hole, this is still something that can be hoped for;
yet a human body is difficult to find. You have already achieved this fruit—do not give rise to arrogance.
The five pleasures among humans are illusory, false, and not real;
one should instead establish heavenly merit to dwell in the Trāyastriṃśa Palace, with halls made of the seven treasures and eating ambrosia.
Those who wish to obtain this and receive heavenly blessings should, during the half-month [of the fast], [practice accordingly].
They reverently observed the three fasts. At that time, King Śilāvihāra instructed and exhorted them without ceasing;
the entire kingdom was abundant, and the people lived in peace and security.
Any sons or daughters who encountered that king were, after their lives ended, all reborn in the heavens.
King Aśoka questioned the messenger: "Is the governance of the Dharma for the benefit of all carried out according to the Dharma?
Are the people throughout the realm entirely submissive?
You must now explain this in detail; there is no need for hesitation or difficulty. The messenger was filled with joy.
Then he spoke forth of his own accord: "May the Great King live long; may the myriad people receive the benefit of the Dharma.
May the Holy King’s vital strength remain robust and firm as he constantly governs and transforms the Western regions through the True Dharma.
Within this stone chamber city, it shall be like the palace of the Heavenly Emperor."
The king ruled therein like Śakra, the King of Devas; the land of Gandhāra was abundant and its people prosperous.
Their conduct was truthful, free from deceit, and they abstained from killing and stealing, following the True Dharma as did all the classes of people.
He sighed with immeasurable joy, wishing that the Great King might enjoy infinite longevity and that, through the Sage’s virtue, all might find peace in their respective places.
Upon hearing this, King Aśoka was filled with delight and gladness; with a serene and joyful countenance, he addressed Yaśas, saying:
I have obtained great benefit; his virtue is truly manifest.
Prince Fayi governs and transforms through principle, leading by the prohibitions of ritual and guiding with benevolence.
The people of this realm all revere and obey him; now it is time to divide this [kingdom].
Of Jambudvīpa, I shall take one portion; one portion I bestow upon my son,
so that my Dharma may flourish and he may enjoy long life and longevity,
governing and transforming the people no differently than now, as far as the Sindhu River to the kingdom of Sāka.
The city of Gandhāra, the village of Oṭṭaka, Kambhoja, An-hsi, Kang-ju, and Wu-sun;
Kucha and Khotan, reaching even to the land of Qin—this is half of Jambudvīpa.
To these he granted the benefit of the Dharma, providing governance for the people.
Leaving a name for future generations— Sīha, Tāmra, Magadha, Kinnara, Vaiśālī, and Vārāṇasī;
the naked ones and those with long ears— from the northern borders of the Snowy Mountains to the edge of the ocean,
I have personally instructed and transformed them, so that there shall be no limit.
The minister Yaśas heard [the king’s words] as if he had been struck by a poisoned arrow;
outwardly feigning a smile while inwardly harboring resentment, he immediately knelt and replied:
“I shall respectfully carry out Your Majesty’s command and transmit the order at once; I dare not delay. Yet, I privately reflect upon my origins...”
Afflicted by the resentment of past enmity, his three poisons were rampant; he disregarded his own life and limb.
"In the past you struck my head, and that pain is difficult to forget.
If I do not now avenge this grievance, when will it ever be fulfilled? Having said this, he immediately withdrew and returned to his dwelling.
He secretly dispatched an attendant to report the matter in full to the Mother of the Gods. Having heard this, the Queen commanded Yaśas:
"Quickly compose a secret edict; withdraw from your position and impose punishment so that no outsider may observe or hear it.
Should anyone witness or hear of it, let them be dealt with according to the law."
Both [the king and the queen] were also overwhelmed with grief. Yaśas addressed them, saying: "The preparation of the secret documents is easy;
we require only the golden seal to affix it to the letters. The Queen replied: "As for the seal, that is my concern;
I shall now provide it. Why worry that it will not be accomplished?"
One who acts with virtuous reflection may be entrusted with a mission; do not act rashly so that matters are leaked abroad.
At that time, the minister Yaśas falsely claimed it was the King’s command and privately conveyed the Sage’s intent, employing myriad deceptive words to treat that land with contempt and guile.
If you wish to reduce [this land] to ashes, say: "King Aśoka has been moved to wrath against that country.
If you wish to bring peace to this Jambudvīpa, quickly follow my command; do not dare to disobey it.
Upon seeing this letter of mine, as well as the seal and closure, [you shall comply].
Having suppressed the Dharma and its benefits, he gouged out both eyes. "This is not my son;
I am not his father. Within the realm over which he ruled, there was likewise nothing that belonged to him;
having secretly composed this book, he went to show it to the Queen and requested that she prepare a precious seal.
There is no need for further doubt or difficulty. Now that the seal has been obtained, I shall dispatch a messenger tomorrow;
should there be even a slight delay, I fear the matter will be exposed.
At that time, the lady immediately wept before the king on that very day, feigning the occurrence of an ominous portent.
Last night while lying down, I had a dream that was most inauspicious;
I fear Your Majesty’s person may encounter illness. You should take precautions in advance to ward off this evil dream.
I pray you drink sweet nectar to gladden my heart, for by doing so, I shall be able to subdue the malevolent spirits.
As an omen of ill fortune, neither the sovereign, nor the subjects, nor the people shall ever again have cause for sorrow.
The King then declared, "This dream is not true; how could it cause my own person to suffer from illness?
Upon hearing this, the Queen wept once more with renewed grief.
Wailing toward the heavens and rolling upon the ground, she said:
"May Your Majesty deign to show compassion and accept my wine; do not let this servant lose her very life forever.
At that time, the King smiled and slowly told her: "It is your own wish that it be so."
"You must drink this! How could I possibly cause you to lose your own life?
This is but a small matter; I shall not oppose you. The King then accepted the wine and drank it slightly more than usual;
he soon became intoxicated and fell asleep, remaining entirely unconscious.
The lady took the seal and used it to close and inspect the letter.
At that time, none of the attendants saw her. The king saw her in a dream;
someone was untying the seal, whereupon he suddenly woke up and asked his attendants, "I have only just begun to sleep peacefully."
My mind and consciousness are tranquil; who comes to disturb me? My spirit cannot find peace—quickly investigate this!
Let there be no falsehood; there must surely be a plot to endanger my life.
He holds a sharp sword in his hand, and brandishes a flying iron wheel.
Displaying the majestic power of heaven, he spoke to the lady, saying:
"Who has commanded you to take my precious seal? If you do not reveal this at once, you shall perish right now.
The lady was filled with fear; she knelt down for a long time and said: "I pray that Your Majesty will deign to examine me."
In truth, there was no such feeling; the King’s anger grew even more intense, and he spoke to him again:
"There is no one else who has provoked or offended me.
Since you do not face me now to confess your transgression with sincerity, I shall take your body and divide it into two parts."
The lady wept and, kneeling, addressed the King, saying:
"This is merely a strange omen manifested as a dream or illusion. Your seed is no ordinary or trivial thing;
how could I, solitary, destitute, naked, and shallow, dare to speak falsely before the King, feigning reality? Even if you require a seal..."
"How could one obtain such things through theft? One must report this with sincerity to the King; how else could it be obtained?
When the King heard these words, he remained silent and did not respond.
He returned to his bed and slept until dawn before awakening. The lady then urgently commanded the false minister, Yaśas:
He swiftly dispatched a messenger; there was no need for delay.

At that time, Prince Dharmapāla, together with his various ministers, had gathered in the palace hall for a joyful assembly and recreation, enjoying themselves as they pleased, when the letter arrived.
Within the city of Śilāgṛha, the king heard from outside that his father-king had issued a command;
he immediately rose and went forward to meet him, prostrating and kneeling to receive it upon the crown of his head.
He entrusted it to his attendants to open the seal, and upon seeing the sovereign’s decree, he found it to be most solemn and urgent.
"He is called King Aśoka; he has brought universal wrath upon this land.

If you wish to dwell securely in the city of Śailaguhā, quickly search for the prince, gouge out both his eyes, and do not let him linger so that even his shadow may shift away. Having heard this, Dharmaya..."
I threw myself upon the ground: "What fault have I committed?
Regarding this letter and command sent by my father the King, which would destroy both my eyes—could it be that someone has slandered me to the King?
When the ministers and the people hear these urgent instructions..."
All were struck with alarm and did not know what to do. "What a terrible calamity it is that such a transformation has appeared!
The Great King was filled with wrath, and among his ministers there were none left to carry on his lineage.
Some of the ministers made this argument: "We dare not [speak further]."
Who is this person that dares to destroy the eyes of the Dharma King?
Who could dare to conceive such an intent as to gouge out both eyes?
You all must assemble together and firmly defend our borders; announce this far and near, and prepare the instruments of war.
It would be better to lose our people, to be separated from our wives and children, than to let our lord suffer such agony.
Strike the drums at once! Summon generals from beyond the borders!
Burn this letter with fire! Destroy and kill the messenger! He is not our lord!
"I am not a subject of his; truly, I do not obey his commands.
By destroying the eyes of the Sage-King, he has harmed the temporal law that benefits all. He addressed his ministers, saying:
'Do not harbor such thoughts as to resist the holy teaching. The military forces of the Father-King are beyond all calculation.'"
Brave, fierce, and robust—rare indeed in this world!
Although you all wish to manifest your humble sincerity, if the matter is not accomplished, the entire realm will perish;
what constancy is there in my life? To whom does this body belong, that it should cause such distress to the Great King?
My resentment is so deep that I would sooner sacrifice my own life than receive the command you have brought;
how could I possibly save myself? It would cause the country to fall into ruin and chaos.
You all must no longer think back upon our previous discussion; quickly accept the King’s instruction and gouge out my eyes.
Indeed, that which flourishes must decline; that which meets must part.
Since there is no self, death cannot be avoided—is this not what the Buddha taught? This body is a vessel of suffering, a place of constant leakage and foulness;
there is not a single thing in it worth craving. Quickly announce this within the city!
"Who is able to endure taking the king’s law for his own benefit and pluck out both eyes?
To him I shall now grant a precious necklace worth ten million, along with gold and silver beyond measure, as well as the kingdom and its people. When the people heard this command, they were moved.
The gates of the Palace of Convergence were blocked; they could not swallow down the needles they had cast.
Of different forms yet with a common aim, they all raised their voices together, crying out to Heaven and striking the earth, each lamenting:
"How extreme is this cruelty! We have lost our Holy King; such is the fate of this celestial palace!"
How transient is this! Such are the cities and fortresses;
before long, the fields will fall into ruin, and the kingdoms and territories shall all become mere mounds of earth.
We shall proclaim together to our neighboring states that King Aśoka was the foremost of evildoers.
To kill one's own son for the sake of fame—what is there to be valued in that?
Since you do not even love your own child, what can the people rely upon?
At that time, within the city, there was an ordinary man who had long harbored a minor grudge against the prince; he stepped straight forward.
Seeking to accept a heavy reward, he said, "I am capable of gouging out his eyes and can also behead him.
The ministers on the left and right pointed him out and addressed [the king], saying, "This man claims he is capable of destroying the King's eyes;
this still merits careful consideration, for he defies the instructions of his father, the King."
"I pray that my lord shall not suffer this bitter agony. When the king saw this man, his grief and weeping were intermingled;
looking around at his attendants, he addressed the ministers, saying:
"I have resided in this city for twelve years, yet I am fully aware of my own faults and shortcomings."

May you all together grant me your understanding and forgiveness. Now that I have regained my sight, when you previously destroyed my eyes, do not again harbor grief or distress, nor give rise to any evil thoughts.
Return to the affairs of state as was your former custom, governing and transforming the people with rectitude, and strive to ensure that all things are done appropriately.
Even if you wish to enjoy the blessings of the heavens, you must always maintain the precepts of fasting and purification without violating them for even a moment.
The King then removed his jeweled crown, his pearl necklaces, and his precious sandals,
and bestowed them upon the person before him, saying, "You should know this of me."
Desiring to contemplate the root of phenomena, he plucked out his eyes one by one and placed them in the palm of his hand.
At that time, that wicked man drew a sharp sword from his hand and first plucked out one eye, placing it into the King’s palm.
The King took the eye himself and contemplated it with deep reflection.
I then recalled the instructions originally taught by my former teacher; suddenly, my mind attained awakening and I held it fast in my thoughts without forgetting.
What my teacher had previously expounded was of the utmost depth and far-reaching significance, and he told me:
"The eye is impermanent. My teacher charged me with the utmost sincerity.
Truly without falsehood, tranquil and subtly discerning, one understands the meaning of impermanence:
this eye will not last long; it is destined for decay. I know that the eye is fundamentally a deceiver of the world, which the masses of fools indulge in and practice, unaware that it is empty.
Birth and death are defiled and turbid, like a plantain tree; though its leaves cover one another, there is no solidity within.
When the wise observe this, they find not a single thing to crave—how could they again give rise to the intent to be attached to the forms of the eye? The eye is not mine.
Neither made nor created, it is devoid of self; how then could there be an eye?
The fool gives rise to delusion and becomes deeply attached to visual consciousness.
Thus they revolve in the dark sea of the long-flowing stream. Now, O Eye, you shall forever part from me.
From what fundamental source did it arise? It serves as my eye. Like bubbles upon the water, rising and ceasing in an instant, it is deceptive and lacks reality.
What use is the fleshly eye for such a phenomenon? Observe minutely the origin of the eye; contemplate its profound mystery.
The mind does not waver; it maintains correctness and restrains disorder.
The mind is like a vajra, and all perceptions are forever stilled; the will does not run toward external objects.
At that time, that person again takes a sharp sword and plucks out his second eye, placing it in the king’s palm.
He contemplated deeply the origin of the eye: from what did it originally arise?
Understanding that all phenomena are quiescent and that the myriad things return to transformation, he attained the supernormal power of the divine eye while sitting upon his seat;
with all defilements exhausted, he personally realized the stage of the Path and moved heaven and earth through his spiritual resonance.
The earth shook in six ways, and joy welled up within him.
He thrice uttered words of praise, casting off the defiled eyes of the world to attain these pure eyes.
As his merit became subtly manifest and he knew for himself that the Way was accomplished, the ministers cried out in lamentation and rolled upon the ground.
"How grievous is this pain! We have lost our heavenly lord.
What conditions were created in the past, what karmic retribution from former lives, that today these eyes should be destroyed?
Some cast away tiles and stones, while others pressed their palms together again; each spoke forth their plea, saying, "We pray the King will look upon us with compassion."
Returning to govern this realm, we shall lead one another to the presence of our father-king to petition him on our behalf and present our case,
so that he may manage the kingdom. At that time, the King’s Dharma will be further comforted,
and he will express his gratitude to the ministers, feeling a profound sense of indebtedness toward the common people.
A man whose form is ruined—how can he find peace in a noble state?
It is fitting that he withdraw of his own accord and depart from the borders of the kingdom at this time.
Taking his wife and a single attendant, he suddenly abandons the throne and departs upon the road, wandering through villages and hamlets.
Traveling on foot through the wilderness across commanderies, counties, kingdoms, and towns,
he encountered the hardships of treacherous and rugged terrain. Yet the Prince, who had long been skilled at playing the lute—
its exquisite and pure tones being rare in the world— relied upon this art to beg for alms from house to house.
Traveling from kingdom to kingdom, he sustained his life by such means;
thus he passed through various districts and cities until he gradually arrived at the domain ruled by his father, the king.
At that time, a foul and evil reputation concerning King Aśoka had spread beyond the seas.
The two eyes of our child have been destroyed; throughout the villages, districts, and kingdoms, there is none who is not shaken with alarm.
We all must consider: where can we find refuge? Men and women, great and small alike, weep as they face one another.
What crime or fault has the Prince committed against the King?
How could that man have escaped with his hands unsevered?
He has seized my noble king and destroyed these two eyes. Prince Dharmavardhana addressed the people:
"Our father the king is without fault; the world holds no grudge against him. This is my own karmic retribution from former lives."
Now he receives this retribution; this causal connection is long-standing.
It was not merely in the present life that King Aśoka, while atop a high tower, was sleeping alone with his consort, whereas Prince Dharmavivardhana stayed within the horse stable.
Throughout the night they sang and played, delighting themselves by plucking the lute.
When the King heard the sound of the lute, his mind was struck with melancholy and his thoughts were transformed. "The notes of the *gong* and *shang* are so harmonious and elegant;
who is this playing the lute? Its resonance is so powerful—it could well be him."
"Is my Dharma beneficial? The man replied: "This is no prince nor one blind by birth;
he lives by begging for alms. The kingdom of Gandhāra is like the palace of Śakra, ruling over the western regions like the sun piercing through the clouds."
At this time the King arose and went to the hall to attend to his duties. The ministers gathered together, desiring to have audience with the Sovereign;

they sought to serve the King, yet as he entered and exited with a mind preoccupied by other thoughts, they were trembling with fear, dreading that calamity might fall upon them. Then the King again heard their voices.
At the sound of the lute being played, he immediately started up;
observing the direction from which it came, he looked toward his attendants and said, "This is no ordinary person;
this must surely be my son who has arrived here. Shoo! You wretched woman, there is no need for further words."
"Quickly bring this man so that I may see him. He immediately dispatched a messenger to summon him to the king's presence.
When the king saw him approaching from afar, he threw himself upon the ground, crying out to heaven and lamenting his grievance;
his mind was utterly distraught, and he was overcome with grief and sorrow.
As if he were being consumed by fire, the ministers sprinkled him with water;
they helped him rise and sit, adjusted his crown, and dressed him in formal attire, then asked him: "Who has destroyed your eyes?
Such bitter agony as this wounds my heart and liver; what use is there for you to remain alive?"
Originally possessing the divine eye, now encountering this calamity;
choked with grief and breath cut short, he dies and then revives. Again grasping his precious crown, he casts it to the ground;
with disheveled head and scattered hair, he brandishes celestial majesty, [casting off] his pearls and jeweled necklaces.
Each standing in a different place, holding a sharp sword in his hand, he addressed those around him, saying:
"I must now utterly destroy the world; neither the old nor the young, neither the weak nor the strong, shall escape my hand. All the people of Śilāvatī shall be devoured by me."
Among the classes of people, this one plucks out my eyes; it causes the kingdom of Gandhāra to become a desolate wilderness.
It sits and ruins my breath, and it shall likewise harm these pure eyes.
In the country where I dwell, it makes no distinction between men and women.
They gouged out all his eyes and immediately hurled iron wheels, which spun through the air and slaughtered every living being within Jambudvīpa.
His father, the king, shedding tears, asked the prince: "Who has destroyed your eyes, bringing you to such a state?"
It causes my heart and liver to break into fragments and snap asunder;
among the billions of onlookers, there is none who does not feel compassion. The Prince then replied, writing and sealing this urgent edict:
"None fail to be struck with alarm; I pray that Your Majesty will not hold me accountable."
The people of Śilāgṛha were kind and harmonious, free from transgression or fault;
yet this son, being of meager merit, brought about this calamity.
All was due to the retribution of his past unwholesome deeds. When the ministers saw the letter, they were all filled with indignation.
What has Aśoka done? He has committed this act of inhumanity;
truly, he has no compassion for Jambudvīpa. How could he have conceived such a mind?
Let us all join together to destroy this prince and spread the word throughout the realm.
Fully prepare the weapons of war; it would be better to lose the realm than to let the prince suffer such humiliation and punishment.
Order the burning of the letters and the execution of the messenger, and at the city of Śilāgṛha, quickly beat the drums for battle.
"He is not my master, nor am I his servant; truly, I did not dare to destroy the prince’s two eyes. The son then offered this instruction:
"The people of that realm must not harbor such thoughts as to resist the holy teaching; why [behave thus] toward your father, the King?"
They give rise to rebellious hearts; from antiquity until now, the cycles of rise and fall have been limited by time.
In honoring the elders and showing respect to the juniors, they receive and uphold the solemn teachings.
Do not delay or disobey these written commands. The masses of the common people are deluded and ignorant, unable to distinguish between the true and the false.
I pray that Your Majesty will show forbearance and grant forgiveness for my shortcomings.
Great King, please take heed and contemplate the Buddha’s words: patience is a great power, capable of overcoming all enmity.
You may release him now, not holding his transgressions against him; do not regard him as your own son.
Giving rise to a murderous intent brings the agonies of hell;
one must endure the bitter suffering of interrogation and scourging as the retribution for one’s sins. What is the use of remembering your son?
If you were to see one who is compassionate and would grant your original vow, why would you harm the people by killing your own son?
The men and women of the land, the various classes of the populace, were all filled with terror;
may you grant them timely pardon and release. At that time, the prince and his preceptor, leading the bhikṣus, entered the city to beg for alms, holding their alms-bowls in their hands.
His dharma-robes were neatly arranged, and he proceeded gradually in due order until he reached the gate of the royal palace.
Aśoka saw him from afar and was overcome with a mixture of grief and tears;
he immediately rose to meet him, knelt down for a long time, and inquired after his well-being: "Formerly, you were a venerable disciple, Prince Dharmavivardhana."
Now having encountered this calamity and misfortune, my two eyes have been destroyed; my grief and sorrow are so piercing that they are difficult to bear.
I pray that the Honored One will deign to look upon me and heal me with the medicine of the Dharma.
The Arhat replied: "Impermanence undergoes a hundred transformations; this has come for a long time."
This was not merely for the present; seeking out a bhikṣu, he immediately approached his seat and commanded the king to summon Fayi. The king personally took his hand and led him forward.
Among the tens of thousands of onlookers, there were none whose hearts did not ache with grief.
He approached to prostrate at his feet, and with tears like a rushing river, choked with grief and indignation, he spoke with humble devotion:
"Formerly, the Teacher’s instruction was indeed as the Tathāgata commanded:
that what possesses eyes is impermanent and lacks any solidity. Reflecting upon this meaning..."
Profound and far-reaching, yet the impure physical eye cannot rely upon it;
it is like a mass of foam, like dew when the sun shines, like bubbles floating on water, or a reflection that shifts with the light.
It is like a plantain tree, a mirage in the wild, or a magical illusion—unreal and insubstantial.
"Abandoned by the wise, what is there to crave? King Aśoka then knelt before him and said:

'I pray you, expound the supreme flavor, so that those like me—whose eyes are restored to sight yet whose hearts are filled with sorrow, grief, and resentment—may be cleansed in the pure depths and freed from the state of drifting and wandering.'"
He sent [the messenger] back to return to the truth, reflecting upon the Honored One’s teaching and dwelling peacefully in non-action.
This shall cause future generations to know the origins of their past lives.
The Arhat then rose and went to the prince’s location, holding a white cotton cloth in his hand to cover Fayi’s head.
Lady Candraprabhā, the mother of the Prince, immediately rose from her seat and knelt with palms joined in service.
She personally held aloft an incense burner, burning various famous incenses toward the lands of the ten directions and all the deities within those realms.
The noble and powerful kings of ghosts have all assembled here; may they bear witness to this vow of utmost sincerity so that my Dharma may flourish. May their eyes be restored.
Witnessed by all the deities, this vow of utmost sincerity moves them deeply, and the eight classes of spirits immediately respond.
Gathering from all four directions, there was no empty space left. He further addressed the prince, saying:
"Arouse your aspiration and take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;
in the honored teachers and elders, and in all the Buddhas of the past and those yet to come. Surrender yourself and take refuge in them."
Arousing a heart of reverence, listen to me, O worthy ones!
I have made a true vow to reach non-attachment and attain the pure eye;
since I attained the Way, I shall never eat first, but will surely deliver others before I take my meal.
I recall that in the past, while serving various Buddhas—
namely Śikhin, Viśvabhū, and Vipaśyin Tathāgatas— I made offerings by means of various kinds of silk banners,
flower canopies, and performances of music and dance, and furthermore, I lit lamps.
Continuing the Radiance of the Honored One, by virtue of this root of merit, may the faculty of sight be restored.
Formerly, under the Buddha Śikhin, he made this vow: "For all those who lack the physical eye, I shall heal them and restore their faculty of sight, so that it is no different than before."
If my vow is fulfilled and I obtain the purity of the eye-faculty,
and if this prince has indeed been my son for five hundred lifetimes, may it be true and not false;
by means of my present body, may I no longer undergo conception, and may I cause the prince [to attain his goal].
"Just as I am, so he is no different. He further addressed Aśoka:
"The King recalled how in the past he offered a single handful of earth to the Tathāgata.
By virtue of this field of merit, the King alone traverses Jambudvīpa with an iron wheel, without rival."
"Now I too shall make a vow of utmost sincerity, that its merit may reach the prince so that he may obtain the faculty of sight.
At that time, the Venerable One ascended into the void and performed the eighteen miraculous transformations; emerging and submerging at will, the Great King beheld him.
With palms joined and kneeling long, he concentrated his mindfulness; casting himself upon the ground, he took refuge in my Honored One, Śākyamuni Buddha.
Having received the remaining blessings, he shall preside over Jambudvīpa.
If the Tathāgata would grant me a prediction of enlightenment, [I shall do so].
When a hundred years have passed since my departure,
there shall arise a king in Jambudvīpa who will erect eighty-four thousand divine temples for the Tathāgatas throughout the entire realm,
just as the divine mouth has spoken; this has now been fully realized and has spread across the land.
Universally arising meritorious deeds, he governs the realm of Jambudvīpa; Walking alone with sovereign freedom, he establishes the Dharma without fail.
Having attained purity of the faculty of sight, his past plantings of merit were offered to the True Persons;
He reverently served the Triple Gem as a National Preceptor and a Master of the Way.
And he bestowed gifts upon the destitute and those who were naked; by means of this meritorious deed, he gave to the prince.
The king recalled his former travels as he journeyed through the realms of his kingdom and passed over various mountains; beyond the Cakravāḍa range, he heard a sound from below.
Thunder shakes heaven and earth; the sounds are mournful and piercing, their tones most bitter and cruel.

The King does not look on as he beholds King Yama; ministers, officials, aides, and attendants stand by to inquire into the causes of the offenses and the nature of the transgressions committed, whereupon he immediately passes judgment.
Administering punishment according to the offense, with a mind free from increase or decrease:

The eighteen hells are fiercely blazing and boiling; Surrounded by sixteen cauldrons, A single cauldron, mountains of knives, and forests of swords, Chariots of fire, and glowing embers— The sinners wail and cry out.
With myriad forms of bitter suffering, the King questioned his attendants:
"Who is this person? The ministers replied: "He is the Lord of the Dead.
The King distinguished between good and evil, examined the gravity of offenses, scrutinized calamities and faults, and weighed the wise against the foolish.
At that time, Aśoka addressed his ministers, saying: "Even the King of Death still employs the hells as a means of governance;
how then could I, who am now the sovereign of living beings, fail likewise to employ the hells for the purpose of governing and transforming?"
He questioned his ministers: "Who among you is such a person—so utterly evil and violent as to preside over hell?
The ministers replied: "Only one who is devoid of compassion and has committed the five heinous crimes can create hell—one with yellow hair and red eyes."
With knitted brows and swollen cheeks, high foreheads and prominent noses—such as these who commit evil, the wicked king commands his ministers: "Seek out such men;
bring them here at once to report. The ministers immediately galloped forth through the kingdoms, districts, and towns.
He saw by the side of a pond a man weaving woolen cloth; beside him were set bow and arrow as he shot at flying birds;
in front, he scattered poisoned rice to catch flocks of sparrows;
with his feet, he pulled hooks and bait to fish for deep-water fish; and behind him, he had laid out dark snares.
Subtly spying for deer and roe, he cranes his neck at the sound of birds;
he lures in birds and beasts, and when people see him, they find him exactly as described in the recruitment notice.
Your servant has returned to report these facts to the King in accordance with the truth. He wanders about seeking wicked men, and his sincerity is indeed such as this.
The king said, "Excellent! This truly fulfills my wish; having thoroughly investigated this man, he must be capable of managing the affairs of the prison.
The king sent a messenger to summon him, saying, "I wish to see you;
I shall bestow upon you precious jewels as much as you require. The wicked man replied:
"I am a lowly man, possessing no knowledge or wisdom.
The King replied, "I shall appoint you as my messenger. You will surely be promoted to a noble rank;
I wish to have your person to manage the affairs of the hells. The man was filled with joy and immediately returned home.
He related the circumstances of the matter in full to his parents. Upon hearing this, his parents were filled with great sorrow and grief;
each took their child into their arms and would not let them go.
The child’s resolve was fierce and resolute, so he immediately drew a sharp sword and slew his parents.

He abandoned him and departed, going to where the king was. He knelt, prostrated, inquired after his well-being, and paid his respects with courtesy, then stood to one side. The king asked the wicked man, "Your parents are still alive;
since there is no one to look after them, by what means have you been able to come here?"
That man himself confessed: "My parents strictly forbade me, yet I took a sword and slew them, then abandoned them and came here.
The King said, "Alas! Truly a committer of the five heinous crimes, you have even harmed your own parents; on whom else can others rely? He then cast that man aside.
They construct the city of hell with cauldrons of boiling water and sword-trees, surrounding it with walls of molten iron;
they then appoint that person as the lord of hell, establishing various ministers and assistants,
each with their own jurisdiction, just like King Yama, and commanding the hell-wardens.
There shall be those who enter the prison, but none shall be allowed to leave.
Whether they be noble or lowly, powerful or honorable elders—once caught, they shall be punished; do not inquire as to their right or wrong.
Even if my own person should enter within these walls, do not permit me to depart.
Furthermore, out of reverence for the Dharma, he circumambulated the city walls and planted fine fruit trees,
cultivating gardens and pavilions that resembled celestial palaces. At that time, I was practicing the dhūta austerities alone,
begging for alms, and gradually proceeded in due order until I arrived at this city gate.
Seeing from outside fragrant flowers and lush, flourishing trees, they think, "This must be the home of a noble and wealthy person," and immediately enter the gate, desiring to beg for food.
But seeing only those being punished, they are struck with terror and wish to turn back; yet the hell-wardens seize them from the front.
They did not allow me to leave, but led me to the place of the cauldrons, intending to inflict upon me the five poisons.
I pleaded with them again, saying: "Please grant me a little reprieve until noon;
having received your grace, I shall never cease my gratitude. My study of the Way has been shallow, and I have not yet recited the scriptures extensively."
Having received permission to hear [the Dharma], they prostrated to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
An evil man, having given his silent consent, set a date within the period. Before long, a man and a woman sat together and committed the act of sexual misconduct.
They were brought in to be punished and placed inside a mortar.
When struck with a pestle, in the space of a mere moment it turns into foam;
at that time I saw this and thought only of the Buddha’s words: "The body is like a mass of foam—truly indeed these words!
To receive a body within the womb, there must necessarily be such a counterpart.
Though one may encounter Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who can escape this affliction?
I shall now contemplate the meaning of impermanence and distinguish the nine outflows;
furthermore, this impure filth has recently changed its color to that of a white dove—thus I reflect upon this physical form.
Like a long-buried heap of bones, subject to manifold transformations, he realized through his mind in an instant that all is like an illusion or a magical creation.
His outflows were exhausted and his fetters untied; joy filled his inner being and manifested outwardly.
"How wonderful is this karmic reward! It brings parting from birth and death."

My mind is tranquil and settled; my will is like a diamond. Though heaven be scorched and earth consumed until they melt into a single unity, and though a blazing fire fills the heavens, how could it burn me?
The wardens of hell urge me on again, and I enter the boiling cauldron; at that time, I simply smile.
Their complexions became joyful and serene, while the hell-wardens grew enraged;
four of them were each seized by their two armpits and cast upside down into the cauldron.
The boiling water turned cold and the fire was extinguished, transforming into a refreshing coolness; all tortures, lashings, and beatings came to a complete rest.
Even if one transforms into a thousand-petaled lotus and sits cross-legged within that lotus,
performing the eighteen miraculous transformations— sitting, reclining, emerging, and submerging—
or flies through the air at a height of seven *zhang* above the ground, the hell-wardens will see this and be struck with terror.
He addressed King Aśoka: "The wonders within this prison are such as have never been seen before.
I pray that Your Majesty will deign to bend your steps for a moment to the city of Niraya and inspect these calamitous marvels.
The King said to the wicked man: "I have a prior commitment; even if I were to enter..."
Nor may you depart from the teaching of the Wheel-Turning King;
since it is said there is no duality, how could I now re-enter this gate? The official said to the king:
"Simply enter, there is no harm; grant me one day's leave, and thereafter a further limit shall be set."
The king then followed him inside and saw a man within the cauldron, sitting cross-legged upon a lotus flower. The king asked from afar, "Who are you?
I replied, "I am a bhikṣu. The king asked again:
"You are now in prison; you ought to be called a criminal. Why do you call yourself a bhikṣu?
At that time, I told you: 'You are truly a fool! By receiving the grace left behind by the Sage, you shall rule as king over the southern continent of Jambudvīpa.
Only after accumulating merit for eternal kalpas will you finally attain this.'"
Now he further slanders the Noble One, calling him a criminal prisoner.
The King asked the ascetic, "For what reason do you now, before the Wheel-Turning King, call me a fool?
At that time, I replied: "When you were a child, with a handful of soil..."
He presented [the clay] to the Tathāgata, who accepted it and offered a blessing.
He then went to the Kāśyapa Temple and mixed water with the clay to repair the southern wall of the temple. He recorded:
"In the future, you shall become a Wheel-Turning King in Jambudvīpa in the south, named Aśoka."
Within a single day, you would have established eighty-four thousand shrines for the Tathāgatas; yet now, in this prison,
you have instead brought about calamity and boundless sin, with your consciousness utterly deranged.
Enveloped by a mind of delusion, you are the most foolish among fools;
no one is more deeply attached than you, O King, nor will you change until death. Now that I have called you a fool, what further delusion remains?
The King’s mind was immediately awakened, and he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground.
He immediately repented of his own transgressions and took refuge in my person.

Thereupon, he ceased all imprisonment and established the roots of goodness, seeking to attain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). He planted the seeds of the fundamental nature of the non-arising and non-ceasing Dharma;
thus has he now attained the rank of a king within the field of merit of the Buddha.
Purifying all defilements and binding the boundaries of his realm, he offered them up to the Triple Gem.
Having truly cultivated such merit, he attained the faculty of sight.
When the King and his venerable teacher made a most sincere vow, he immediately obtained perfectly pure eyes while remaining upon his seat.
The various devas, the spirits, and the kings of ghosts all exclaimed, "Excellent!
This is unprecedented! They marveled at this inconceivable response to divine inspiration.
Immediately, they unfolded their layered robes and gazed with eyes wide open upon the King and his consort.
From afar he beheld Fayi, whose countenance was extraordinary and rare in the world.
At that time, heaven and earth shook in six ways; mountains, rivers, and rocky cliffs surged and subsided.
With joy swelling within his breast, he could not contain himself.
Previously, kneeling with palms joined, I addressed the Celestial Master, saying: "Master, you are like a living Buddha who bestows eyes upon men.
By the power of the blessings you have received, I have been reborn with pure eyes;
the King beholds auspicious responses that are beyond description. This must surely be a celestial body."
He placed [the crown] upon my ear and removed his own precious diadem, bestowing it upon Dharmodgata to succeed as the Wheel-Turning King and govern Jambudvīpa.
The prince knelt before his father and said: "I do not possess such majesty; how could I dare to succeed to the noble throne?"
The Father King said: "Observing your conduct, it is certain you are a celestial deity;
of this I have no doubt. Your remaining under my rule is not appropriate;
you ought to succeed to the throne, while I should serve as your minister. Follow my words at once."
"Accept this precious crown; do not harbor doubts or difficulties, nor give rise to thoughts of hesitation.
The Teacher further addressed him, saying: "The King should accept this celestial crown.
Its majestic appearance shall govern and transform for six years. Formerly, when he was originally a king, it lasted for sixty thousand years."
At that time, he was six years short; his deficiency did not suffice for the required number.
King Aśoka, filled with doubt, addressed the Great Master, saying: "I pray you, explain the fundamental causes.
What deeds were performed in a former life to bring about such noble and exalted status? Since he has now become my son..."
My eyes have attained pure clarity; though they were once impaired, I have now regained them whole.
By what further cause and condition did I encounter the Honored One? Guided by this Dharma Master, I have attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Now I am a son of the Buddha; all defilements and impurities have been extinguished.
Having further attained the Way and forever departed from birth and death, he wished to speak of the fundamental practices he had undergone in the past.
The Teacher said to the King: "Listen to what I say and reflect upon it with careful attention.
Regarding the causes and conditions of the past, in ages long gone..."
Ninety-one kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin Tathāgata.
At that time, the prince became my son; he was skilled in mathematics, arts, and painting. For seven days, I made offerings to that Buddha.
The prince painted and fashioned an image of the Tathāgata.
By means of that image, he proclaimed the Most Victorious One; the Tathāgata praised him, saying, "Truly, you are without peer.
Thereupon, before that Buddha, he gave rise to the resolve and made a vow: "In every place where I am born..."
May you never fall into the evil realms; may you always be handsome and upright, with clear and intelligent eyes.
May you be born into a noble family and never dwell in a lowly or base station.
May you always be loved and respected by women, such that all who behold you shall prostrate themselves upon the ground.
Subsequently, there was a Buddha named Śiṅga Tathāgata.
Together with his bhikṣus, he traveled to the city of Viśālā. At that time, I was a householder;
this was my place of rest, where I again made offerings and served Śiṅga Buddha. The next Buddha was named...
Under the Tathāgata Anupamapatra, he delivered and liberated countless beings.
At that time, seeking a vow, he offered a lamp for his father; for seven days and seven nights, the light was never extinguished.
By virtue of this merit, he has long been free from suffering and affliction.
In whatever place he was born, he attained the purity of the divine eye.
During this Bhadrakalpa, a Buddha appeared in the world named Kuśana;
he delivered immeasurable people, possessed the thirty-two marks, had a complexion like refined gold, and sat beneath the tree of enlightenment.

Having subdued the hosts of Māra and his enemies, for sixty-six years he upheld the prohibitive precepts for three months and six years, never once failing or losing them. Next there was another Buddha,
the Honored One Kanakamuni, who illuminated the world like the full moon.
At that time, I was also the body of an elder; the prince became my youngest son.

Subsequently, there was a Buddha named Kāśyapa, endowed with all the marks of excellence, who appeared in the world.
At that time, I was once again a great and wealthy householder, extensively receiving his grace and kindness.

Because in the past he slandered a true person—an Arhat—while looking on at a woman, and because of that original evil deed, he sought to destroy the eyes of others.
Now, though my two eyes are destroyed, the retribution for good and evil shall never decay.
I request Kāśyapa and his assembly of bhikṣus; for seven days, I shall provide whatever offerings they require.
My son likewise, for seven days and seven nights, shall do the same.
I pay homage to the Tathāgata and the assembly of noble ones.
Holding lamps aloft with both hands, my body remaining motionless, I repent three times each day, taking refuge in the Buddha:
"Whatever deeds I have previously committed through body, speech, and mind, I now renounce them all."
I reverently cultivate the prohibitions and precepts; may I, in the future, should I encounter such a Holy Honored One as this, be permitted to meet and pay homage to him.
May I reach the end of suffering within that very assembly, and at the same time as my father, become an Arhat.
Under the Buddha Vipaśyin, he burned lamps for seven days; having made a vow to seek merit, he obtained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Although it has now been destroyed, the very root of his physical eye is immediately attained as the retribution for that divine eye. Having now encountered Kāśyapa...
When he arises in the world, may I be born again so that I may obtain the eye of purity; or perhaps at some time, having established a firm vow,
may I attain enlightenment simultaneously with my father, and for six years govern as a King of True Dharma.
"When these numbers have been completed, one shall then exhaust all outflows.
Upon hearing these words, the king gave rise to a virtuous mind; he immediately knelt before him, prostrating himself upon the ground:
"The World-Honored One is now pure, free from all defilements and attachments within the Dharma of the Noble Ones."
Abiding peacefully in the unconditioned, the Dharma benefits the new king;
he governs Jambudvīpa where there are no thieves or plunderers, no diseases, and no paths of unwholesome karma.
He universally practices a mind of loving-kindness, and all look upon one another with harmonious countenances.
At that time, King Fayi addressed his ministers, saying: "You all must be filial and obedient;
do not harbor wicked or treacherous thoughts. Do not give rise to intentions of killing or stealing.
As for the retribution of unwholesome deeds, do not engage in sexual misconduct, nor speak falsehoods or frivolous words, and let no wine pass your lips."
I shall always accord with the Dharma and never contravene the true teaching; thus I shall attain the traces of the Path.

"I beg to be permitted to leave the household life and cultivate pure conduct. The king immediately granted permission for him to go forth and study.

In this very body, you shall sever all outflows; do not harbor indolence, lest you suffer further humiliation."
Having shaved off his hair and beard, he concentrated his mind and heart.

there was nothing he did not understand as his teacher gradually instructed and exhorted him.
One should follow the proper guidelines; the eyes are like a dream or an illusion.
