I shall now explain for you: their gait is stumbling and faltering; they are unaware of themselves and their vision is clouded by confusion.
They are constantly prone to forgetfulness, and their movements are light, frivolous, and like wandering through a vast wilderness. Such people have come from the Reviving Hell.
The joints and limbs ache with distress; one awakens startled from sleep; in dreams, one comes from the terrible Black Rope Hell;
the hair is coarse and the eyes are distorted; the teeth are long, one is prone to anger, and the voice is turbid, violent, and rapid;
one comes from the Saṃghāta Hell; and the sound of one's speech is loud and high-pitched.
Lacking a sense of shame or remorse, they delight in quarreling and shouting; unable to distinguish truth from falsehood, they groan while lying in bed.
Dreaming repeatedly, they are startled and cry out; one should know that such people have come from the Hell of Wailing.
Constantly fond of weeping and lamenting, they climb to high places to gaze into the distance.
This person is fond of quarreling with their family members, showing no distinction between kin and stranger;
upon speaking, they immediately provoke anger, refusing to eat for days on end. This individual originally came from the Great Wailing Hell;
they are tall in stature but have thin legs, possess meager physical strength, and speak with a constricted throat.
His voice is like that of a breaking jar; his consciousness is unstable;
his mind lacks filial piety—one should know that this person has come from the Avīci Hell.
His body is coarse and ugly, constantly suffering from cold and shivering; he craves heat and delights in thirst; he is stingy, greedy, and envious.
Seeing others practicing generosity, they themselves give rise to affliction; such a person has come from the Hot Hell.
Seeing fire, they are struck with terror, yet they rejoice in warmth and find their gait light and easy.
They do not avoid what is appropriate for the occasion, and they immediately regret whatever they have done.
Furthermore, wishing to bestow [merit] once more, this person again comes from the Great Heat Hell;
they sleep lightly and are prone to anger, forgetting much of what they have received.
Their actions are narrow and limited, lacking a vast and expansive mind; they feel terror upon seeing the great and find joy in the small.
This person has come from the Utpala Hell; with red eyes and a hideous form, they constantly delight in quarreling and litigation, slandering the sages and saints.
They watch day and night for those who have attained the Way to commit unrighteous acts; one should know that this person is such.
Coming from the Paduma hell: one who casts a sidelong glance at a triangle;
such a person, being unfilial toward their two parents, will have a short life upon birth. Coming from the Kumuda hell:
one who is fond of wearing swords and blades and forcibly incites others to fight; such a person will certainly be killed by others. Coming from the Puṇḍarīka hell.
With sores and wounds upon the body, and foul breath from the mouth;
having no kin among men, they come from the vast hells. Their physical forms are massive, yet their gait is feeble and weak;
with scant hair and thin skin, they are constantly beset by many ailments and feel anger whenever they see others.
Greedily devouring without satiety—know that such a person has come from the Hell of Heat;
their body is white with blue eyes, and when they speak, foam flows from their mouth.
Their speech lacks coherence, and they delight in playing with dust and soil; seeing deep, stagnant mud, they lie down upon it.
This person comes from the Ash Hell; with hair curled upward and yellow eyes, he is loathsome for others to behold.
When facing matters, he is filled with panic and fear. Coming from the Sword-Tree Hell, his hands constantly grasp a blade;
he rejoices whenever he hears of a fight, yet is himself harmed by blades.
Coming from the Hell of Blades, their bodies are blackened and withered; they take pleasure in dark chambers and utter evil words.
Coming from the Hell of Hot Ashes, they possess meager strength and scant breath, lacking self-mastery;
whether they gain or lose what is appropriate does not depend on them at all.
If one sees an animal being slaughtered and does not leave its side,
it should be known that this person has come from the Hell of Flaying. If, out of anger and impatience,
one immediately feels remorse and is able to apologize before a day or night has passed, earnestly reproaching one's own heart, [the retribution may be avoided].
As if undergoing punishment, this person comes from the Kūṭa hell;
he delights in foul dwellings, eats coarse and wretched food, and wears hideous raiment.
Coming from the Vaitaraṇī hell, his countenance is ugly and his breath is harsh and foul.
Those who delight in slander and strife will come from the Fragrant Hell;
one should observe the appearance from which they originate and, knowing it, stay far away.
Next, regarding the animals described, their physical forms are diverse and distinct; contemplate them with a focused mind.
They do not create the conditions for that; their speech is slow and hesitant;
they do not give rise to anger and show humility and respect toward elders; they come from among elephants; their bodies are large, hideous, and foul-smelling;
they endure hunger and cold; they are fierce in anger and difficult to appease; they come from among camels.
Traveling far with vigor and strength, Not avoiding perilous difficulties, Recognizing the truth amidst a hundred matters—these come from among horses.

Kindness, harmony, magnanimity, and benevolence, Capable of enduring cold and heat, with actions that leave no trace—these come from among oxen. Loud voice and lack of shame—these come from among sheep.
Affectionate toward many things, unable to distinguish between right and wrong, Coming from among donkeys, with long tusks and great fear, Constantly craving meat; for him, no task is difficult.
Coming from among lions, his body is tall and his eyes are round, He roams through the vast wilderness.
Hating and envying his wife and children, he comes from among tigers;
with long fur and small eyes, he harbors little anger yet delights not in staying in one place.
Coming from among birds, his nature is treacherous and ungrateful; he rejoices in killing insects and finds pleasure alone in burial mounds.
Coming from among foxes, they have faint voices yet are courageous and robust;
they are free from lust and do not cherish wife or children. Coming from among wolves, they do not favor fine clothing and serve to track down those who commit illicit acts;
they sleep little and are prone to anger. Coming from among dogs, [they possess these traits].
Short in stature with long hair, gluttonous and prone to sleep, having no preference for clean places, they come from among pigs;
their fur is yellow and they are impetuous, finding solitary pleasure in mountains and hills while greedily craving fruits and flowers, they come from among monkeys;
they are full of delusions and possess a forced, shameless countenance.
Fearless and untroubled, he knows how to act with reciprocity;
having come from among crows, his nature is full of lustful desire, and he possesses little sense of propriety.
Having come from among pigeons, his mind lacks discernment; his conduct is perverse and contrary, yet he is capable of enduring humiliation.
Unfilial toward one's parents, they come from among the mandarin ducks;
ignorant of both the Dharma and what is wrong, they remain deluded day and night.
Coming from among sheep, they are fond of lust and enjoy idle chatter; they frequently associate with powerful clans and are beloved by the masses.
Coming from among parrots, their actions are impulsive and violent; among performers, they are talkative and tedious.
Coming from among starlings, their gait is slow and deliberate, their minds harbor schemes, and they cause much harm to living beings; they come from among cranes.
Small in stature and fond of lust, their minds are not concentrated or settled. Seeing forms, their hearts are deluded;
they come from among the sparrows. Their eyes are red and their teeth are short;
when they speak, they spit foam, and when they lie down, it entangles their bodies. They come from among the vipers; when they speak, they are full of anger.
Failing to examine the meaning of what comes before, they utter fiery poison from their mouths;
coming from among scorpions, they dwell alone and greedily consume. Their voices are hoarse and gurgling;
coming from among wildcats, they sleep little. They tunnel through walls to commit theft, greedy for wealth and bold in their fears.
There is neither kinship nor estrangement; they have come from among the rats. Contemplate deeply their appearance:
they come from the realm of animals. Next, I shall speak of the hungry ghosts;
listen with focused attention. Their bodies are full of dread; they wrap their hair around their bodies, and their garments are soiled and dusty.
Coming from the realm of hungry ghosts, their lips are parched and their noses are sunken; their throats are narrow and their complexions are yellow.
They delight in perverse conduct and come from the realm of hungry ghosts. They are lustful, stingy, and greedy, envying what others have;
they do not take pleasure in giving and come from the realm of hungry ghosts.
Disrespectful toward one's parents; within the household, large and small alike, conflict and litigation arise whenever they move;
coming from among the hungry ghosts, they do not believe in ultimate sincerity;
their conduct is characterized by meager strength and little wisdom; coming from among the hungry ghosts, their voices are ruined and their hearing is obstructed.
One who frequently gives rise to anger, whose food is always too hot, who has come from among the hungry ghosts and is perpetually lacking wealth,
who is empty, impoverished, destitute, and wretched— such a person is ridiculed by the wise for having come from among the hungry ghosts;
their gate does not serve the Buddha, nor do they delight in hearing the Dharma.
Forever severed from the path to heaven, they come from the realm of hungry ghosts.
Disrespectful toward their wives, children, brothers, and sisters, they are loathed and envied by others.
Born from the realm of hungry ghosts, they are born naked and destitute; no one looks after them, and in the end, they return to their place of origin.
Coming from the realm of hungry ghosts, their minds are narrow and constricted;
they take no pleasure in adornment, and their conduct is ugly. Coming from the realm of hungry ghosts, whatever they do fails to achieve its purpose;
they are driven away by others. Coming from the realm of hungry ghosts.
Rejoicing in success and deprecating failure; Failing to examine the fundamental source; Not accepting the admonitions of others;
Coming from the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*); Having no delight in pure places; Delighting in dwelling in latrines and privies;
With an ugly and filthy countenance; Coming from the realm of wind spirits (*vāyu-deva*); Possessing a massive body and being fond of pleasure.
Constantly craving meat, they take solitary pleasure in spirit shrines; having come from among the yakṣas, they are fierce and prone to fighting.
Greedily attached to whatever they see, they have no sense of fear or restraint;
having come from among the yakṣas, those who see them have their hair stand on end as they advance directly forward and stare intently.
Like one who has lost something, they come from the rākṣasas; their bodies are slender and their skin thin, with a serene and pleasant complexion.
They rejoice upon hearing music. When the gandharvas arrive, their intent is light and buoyant;
they anoint themselves with fragrant incense and possess many arts and skills.
The Gandharvas come; they always delight in song and dance.
Men and women attend them, speaking first and smiling afterward. The Kimnaras come;
their dispositions are gentle and supple, they understand the proper seasons, and they are able to sever the fetters of outflows. The Mahoragas come.
These are the characteristics of hungry ghosts (*preta*), yakṣas, and rākṣasas. Next, one shall explain humans according to their fundamental faculties (*indriya*):
knowing the destination of their rebirth, understanding that what they grasp is not false, and clearly comprehending their activities;
having come from the human realm, they understand all illusions and deceptions.
Having already ceased such actions, their conduct is impartial; the words of good and evil they have encountered since coming from the human realm they never forget.

They do not believe in the treacherous and false that come from the human realm—namely, greed, lust, stinginess, and envy—and though they cling to these in their hearts, it is difficult for them to relinquish them.
Fully understanding worldly customs, they come from the path of humanity;
with faith and a generous mind, they discern what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma. Their minds are without partiality;
coming from the path of humanity, they do not miss the proper seasons, nor are they indolent, but rather revere the sages and worthies.
Coming from the human realm, if one encounters a śramaṇa, one upholds the precepts, is widely learned, and serves them with a sincere heart;
coming from the human realm, one makes offerings to the Buddhas, the True Dharma, and the Saṃgha, and hears the Dharma at the appropriate times; coming from the human realm.
Hearing the Dharma, one is able to understand it; hearing of evil, one does not commit it.
Swiftly attaining Nirvana, having come from the human realm—these are the characteristics of a human being. Having roughly described their appearance, I shall now describe the features of devas.
As for the place they have come from: their eyes are round and their faces are square.
With golden bodies and golden hair, they possess every skill.
When the asuras come, they look straight ahead at the ground without any doubt or difficulty; whenever they see an enemy, they strike back.

Coming from the realm of Śiva, his body is tall and white; his features are upright and handsome, yet he does not favor the radiance of fire.

Coming from the Heaven of No-Thought, the sentient beings of the five destinies each have their own origins;
their temperaments and conducts differ, and their aspirations and characters are distinct.

Extensively expounding the flavor of the Dharma, the subtle and wondrous teaching:
one should deeply contemplate the phenomena of the aggregate of the eye—from where did they originally come? To where do they go?

it must inevitably perish and decay. Form is like a mass of foam;
by its nature, it must disperse. Sound, fragrance, flavor, and phenomena—all are utterly devoid of reality.
